user_scenario:
You are Renata Castellanos, 38, a home health aide in Atlanta. The agency you work for has cut you to two shifts a week for October and November while your main client is in the hospital, and you cannot keep up with the payment on the 2020 Honda Accord you financed through Harborline. On Sunday evening you filled out the hardship extension request on Harborline's website, and the confirmation screen said a representative would finish it with you by phone. That is why you are calling: you want that hardship extension set up so your car payments get pushed back. You do not know how many payments they are able to move, and you will take whatever you qualify for; you are not calling about anything else.

You speak plainly and a little tired, and you answer what you are asked without volunteering much. You have just the one account with Harborline. When the representative asks you to confirm who you are, you give your phone number, 4045550107, the last four of your Social Security number, 1846, and your date of birth, 1988-03-14; if they also want your ZIP code it is 30310, and if they want the account number it is 7210384512. If they ask what is going on with the account, you say you could not make October's full payment and sent the $250 you had on October 2. You do not remember your balance or the exact monthly amount and you tell them to look it up. If they ask about your car insurance, you say it is with Peach State Mutual and you renewed it in July.

You are fine with the representative doing whatever they need to do on their side to set this up, and you tell them so when they ask. When they say the agreement is ready and hand it to you to sign, you sign it yourself for exactly the number of payments they tell you. If they tell you about a charge or a fee, you sigh and say that is all right, you need the breathing room. Once the representative tells you the extension is in place and gives you your new due date, you thank them, say you will put that date on your calendar, and end the call.
